summary: Describes RSVP-TE procedures and extensions for setting up and maintaining label switched paths that cross domain boundaries, in MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to build a planned route that travels through several separate networks, each run by different people.

questions: what is the contiguous lsp bit
contiguous vs nested vs stitched lsp
subtitle: How a traffic-engineered MPLS or GMPLS path can be signaled across several networks, and how the start of the path can insist on one method.

tldr.problem: A traffic-engineered Label Switched Path often has to cross several domains, such as Autonomous Systems or IGP areas, each with its own policies and path computation. RSVP-TE alone does not say how the border nodes should handle that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out the procedures a domain border node follows for policy, signaling method, ERO processing, crankback and RRO filtering. It adds one flag bit, the Contiguous LSP bit, so the ingress can forbid nesting and stitching.
tldr.outcome: Operators get a defined way to choose between contiguous, nested and stitched LSPs per domain, with new error codes for policy and method conflicts. It updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473.

facts.label: Contiguous LSP flag
facts.value: Bit 4 of the Attributes Flags registry

today: RFC 5151 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2008. It updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Inter-Domain Signaling Needs Rules
sections.content:
RFC 5151 describes procedures and extensions for RSVP-TE signaling in MPLS Traffic Engineering packet networks and in GMPLS packet and non-packet networks. Its goal is to set up and maintain Label Switched Paths (LSPs) that cross domain boundaries.

The RFC defines a domain as any collection of network elements within a common realm of address space or path computation responsibility. Autonomous Systems, IGP routing areas and GMPLS overlay networks are all examples. The requirements for inter-area and inter-AS traffic engineering are in RFC 4105 and RFC 4216, and the framework is in RFC 4726.

The signaling here applies to MPLS-TE packet LSPs set up with RFC 3209 and to all LSPs, packet and non-packet, that use the GMPLS extensions of RFC 3473.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine mailing a package through several countries, each with its own customs rules. This RFC writes down how the border officers should handle a package that wants a planned route.

sections.title: Three Ways to Cross Domains
sections.content:
An inter-domain TE LSP can be signaled in three ways, and they can be mixed: each is a per-domain choice. One example in the text runs contiguously through domain B, nests across domain C, and stitches across domain D.

  • Contiguous: one TE LSP set up across all domains with the normal RSVP-TE procedures. It has the same RSVP-TE session and LSP ID at every LSR along its path.
  • Nested: the end-to-end LSP rides inside a hierarchical LSP (H-LSP) across a domain, using label stacking in packet networks, as in RFC 4206.
  • Stitched: shorter LSP segments are joined into one longer LSP, using the procedures of RFC 5150. In the control plane each segment has its own RSVP session.

The choice is a matter of policy for the ingress and for each domain border node. A transit LSR only sees TE LSPs and is unaware of the option. A border LSR must support contiguous LSPs, since that is the default RSVP-TE mode. Not supporting nesting or stitching limits an operator's options but does not stop inter-domain LSPs from being set up.

The extensions needed to signal each LSP type, the routing extensions and the path computation techniques are out of scope for this document.
sections.plainLanguage: You can drive straight through a country, ride in a bus convoy that takes you across, or switch to a different vehicle at each border. Each country can say which of these it allows.

sections.title: What a Domain Border Node Must Do
sections.content:
When a border node receives the RSVP Path message for an inter-domain LSP, it MUST do four things before forwarding it:

  1. Apply domain and node policies. On failure it SHOULD send a PathErr with "Policy control failure" / "Inter-domain policy failure".
  2. Pick the signaling method. Any restriction set by the ingress MUST be obeyed; within that freedom the node MAY choose by local policy. If no method is available it MUST send a PathErr.
  3. Carry out the ERO processing rules, in addition to RFC 3209 and RFC 3473.
  4. Compute the path across the domain and possibly the exit point. For nesting or stitching it also finds or signals an intra-domain LSP to carry the inter-domain one.

The ERO rules include these. Policies on the ERO MUST be applied, for example rejecting EROs that name nodes inside the domain. If an ERO subobject names a TE link formed by an H-LSP or LSP segment, contiguous signaling MUST NOT be used. A loose next hop (an IP address or an AS number) MUST be expanded by path computation. With nothing beyond the local node in the ERO, the egress named in the Session object is treated as the next loose hop.

Path computation itself is not defined here. The RFC points to RFC 5152 and the Path Computation Element approach of RFC 4655 as options.

An ingress can ask for a contiguous LSP to keep maximal control over the path and reoptimization. A transit operator may allow only stitching so it can reoptimize its own domain. The result is a PathErr, and the ingress can avoid that domain, relax its requirements or give up.
sections.plainLanguage: When a traveler reaches a border, the officer checks the rules, chooses how the traveler may cross, reads the planned route, and works out the road to the next stop. If the rules say no, the officer sends back a note saying why.

sections.title: Failures, Crankback and Hiding Details
sections.content:
When setup fails, a PathErr travels back toward the ingress and is seen by each border node in turn. A border node MAY apply policy to limit what it reveals, for example replacing a specific node failure with a general error for the whole domain. But it MUST NOT suppress a PathErr except to attempt rerouting, and non-border nodes SHOULD NOT modify it.

Border nodes are also a natural place for crankback (RFC 4920). A node MAY hold the PathErr and try again with another route or another downstream domain. If a retry succeeds it MUST discard the held error. If all retries fail it MUST send the error upstream.

For the Record Route Object (RRO), a border node MAY filter or modify what it reports, for example swapping the hops inside the domain for the AS number. It MUST NOT hide itself and MUST include itself in the RRO. Filtering does not break signaling, but it can make diagnostics harder and can make procedures such as Fast Reroute less efficient.

Border nodes that want to see Notify messages (RFC 3473) are RECOMMENDED to put their own address in the Notify Request objects. The cost of handling and forwarding those messages grows linearly with the number of domains.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trip fails, the border officers pass the bad news back, and they may keep some details secret. Before giving up, an officer can try a different road.

sections.title: The Contiguous LSP Bit
sections.content:
If a network has one policy for all LSPs, no protocol extension is needed. Where several techniques coexist, the ingress may want to constrain the border nodes. RFC 4420 defines the LSP_Attributes object with an Attributes Flags TLV, and this document adds one bit to it, the Contiguous LSP bit.

When the ingress sets the bit (one), a domain border LSR MUST NOT perform stitching or nesting for that LSP. When it is clear (zero), the border LSR MAY stitch or nest according to local policy. No transit node may change the bit.

  • A node that understands the bit but cannot support contiguous LSPs MUST send a PathErr with "Routing Problem" / "Contiguous LSP type not supported".
  • A node that supports contiguous behavior MUST signal a contiguous LSP. A border node, or a node expanding a loose hop, MUST include an RRO Attributes subobject with the bit set in the Resv RRO, if one is present.
  • Domain border LSRs MUST support and act on the flag.
  • A node that does not recognize the TLV or the bit MUST forward the object unmodified.

What an ingress does after receiving a PathErr is out of scope, but may include computing another path.
sections.plainLanguage: The traveler can put a sticker on the package saying "no switching vehicles." Officers must obey it, and nobody may peel the sticker off.

sections.title: Protection and Reoptimization
sections.content:
The procedures above apply to every inter-domain TE LSP, including bypass tunnels, detour LSPs and segment recovery LSPs. Backup paths with loose hops need ERO expansion, and to keep a backup disjoint the node expanding it needs the protected LSP's path. That comes from RROs, the DETOUR object for Fast Reroute (RFC 4090), or route exclusion (RFC 4874).

For Fast Reroute, protecting a failure inside a domain works exactly as in RFC 4090, and with nesting or stitching the end-to-end LSP is protected by protecting the H-LSP or segment. For a failed link between two domains, a contiguous LSP can use any Point of Local Repair (PLR) and Merge Point (MP), but with stitching or nesting they MUST be domain border nodes. A border node failure is handled by protecting to the far end of the stitching segment or H-LSP. GMPLS segment recovery (RFC 4873) covers the same cases without new extensions.

Reoptimization moves an LSP to a better path using make-before-break. For a contiguous LSP, the ingress MUST initiate it. With nesting or stitching, a change within one domain that keeps the border nodes can be done locally without affecting the end-to-end LSP. End-to-end reoptimization can pick new border nodes but risks more disruption. The mechanisms of RFC 4736 SHOULD be used for contiguous inter-domain LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bridge on the route breaks, there must be a backup road that does not go over the same bridge. And if a better road appears later, the trip can be moved to it without stopping the traffic.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The procedures are described as backward compatible with existing deployments. Ingress LSRs need not support the extensions to set up intra-domain LSPs. A transit LSR that sees a Path message without the Contiguous LSP bit, or without the LSP_Attributes object at all, allows all modes, so older ingress LSRs can still start inter-domain LSPs.

Transit, non-border LSRs do nothing special and pass the LSP_Attributes object on unmodified under the rules of RFC 2205. Domain border LSRs do need an upgrade before inter-domain LSPs are allowed, because policy, administrative and security controls must be in place first. The RRO additions are fully backward compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: Old equipment keeps working. Only the border guards need new training before they let planned routes through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RSVP does not currently provide automated key management, and RFC 4107 states a requirement for it in some situations. Before using inter-domain signaling, administrators of neighboring domains MUST be satisfied that a suitable trust relationship exists. Without one, they SHOULD NOT deploy it and SHOULD disable RSVP-TE on inter-domain interfaces.

Operators SHOULD be given policies and filters at the border for incoming Path messages, a way to rate-limit setup requests or errors from a domain, and policy-based filtering or modification of outbound RSVP messages. Examples in the text: reject or ignore ERO hops inside the domain, hide interior hops in the RRO, change addresses in PathErr or Notify messages, or silently drop a Path message after a path computation failure, since a Path message could be read as a network probe.

Implementations MUST also let operators control optional features that may be a security risk, such as graceful-restart information in Hello messages across a border. OAM tools such as BFD and LSP ping may need their messages intercepted, modified or passed through at borders.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors should only share road access if they trust each other. Each border officer can refuse, limit or quietly ignore requests that look suspicious.
